title: How Southeast Asia Is Navigating a Fragmented Trading System
gist: ASEAN is not replacing China in global supply chains but has become an intermediating production layer between Chinese industrial inputs and U.S./global demand: exports to the U.S. grew 37.5% from 2022-2025 while the bloc's deficit with China hit a record $296 billion in 2025 and widened another 24% to $166 billion in H1 2026. Chinese chip shipments to ASEAN more than doubled to $49.5 billion in H1 2026 while ASEAN's direct chip exports to China halved, and clean-tech imports surged — leaving ASEAN governments trying to reconcile U.S. tariff avoidance, Chinese overcapacity management, and continued access to Chinese inputs.

insights.claim: China accounts for roughly one in every five dollars of ASEAN trade and is the region's dominant source of factory inputs, while the United States is its fastest-growing major export market.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: ASEAN economies carry dual exposure — a demand shock from U.S. tariffs and a cost/supply shock from Chinese input policy hit the same firms.
insights.quote: Diversification away from China has not meant separation: much of the region's manufacturing boom is built on Chinese inputs.
insights.locator: Key Takeaways

insights.claim: Global trade is being rerouted and rewired rather than collapsing under fragmentation, with Southeast Asia as the clearest example of that rewiring.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Fade deglobalization-as-volume-collapse trades; the tradable is the change in routing, freight lanes, and origin-compliance costs, not aggregate trade volume.
insights.quote: Global trade is not collapsing under fragmentation. It is being rerouted and rewired, and Southeast Asia is one of the clearest examples of that shift.
insights.locator: Global trade is not collapsing under fragmentation

insights.claim: ASEAN's trade map inverted over a decade: intra-regional trade fell from nearly a quarter of total trade in 2012 to just over 20% by 2025, the U.S. share climbed above 12%, Japan's share halved, and Taiwan surpassed Japan on the back of the AI boom.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Japan's structural retreat and Taiwan's AI-driven ascent in ASEAN trade reframe which trading partners' cycles now drive Southeast Asian export data.
insights.locator: Southeast Asia's trade map has been redrawn

insights.claim: The same supply chains that make Southeast Asia attractive as an alternative production base expose it to U.S. scrutiny over transshipment, rules of origin, and economic security.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Origin-content rules are the key regulatory risk vector for ASEAN-domiciled exporters — a tariff-evasion crackdown hits the region's growth engine directly.
insights.locator: This creates a new dilemma

insights.claim: ASEAN's trade deficit with China hit a record $296 billion in 2025, more than double the $123 billion level of 2023, and widened a further 24% to $166 billion in the first half of 2026.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A doubling in two years with no sign of mean reversion — expect ASEAN trade-remedy actions and anti-dumping cases against Chinese goods to accelerate.
insights.locator: The bloc's trade deficit with Beijing hit a record

insights.claim: ASEAN's exports to China have plateaued since 2021 while imports from China surged, making the imbalance structural rather than cyclical.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Chinese demand is no longer a marginal growth source for ASEAN exporters; the region's growth is levered to U.S. and AI-infrastructure demand instead.
insights.locator: ASEAN's exports to China have plateaued since 2021

insights.claim: ASEAN's bilateral deficit with China equalled roughly a quarter of China's $1.2 trillion global goods surplus in 2025, making Southeast Asia one of the largest single outlets for China's export surge.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Sizes ASEAN as the marginal absorber of Chinese overcapacity — if the region imposes barriers, China's surplus has to relocate or compress.
insights.locator: The regional imbalance is part of something larger

insights.claim: For the first time all six major ASEAN economies ran deficits with China in 2025, as Singapore — the last in surplus through 2024 — slipped into a small deficit and Indonesia swung from surplus to a nearly $20 billion shortfall.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Universal deficit status removes the last domestic political constituency defending open trade with China in each ASEAN capital.
insights.quote: leaving all six in the red with China for the first time
insights.locator: Beyond the three largest deficits, the trajectories diverged

insights.claim: Vietnam's deficit with China more than doubled to $116 billion, Thailand's nearly doubled to $68 billion, and Malaysia's nearly tripled to $43 billion between 2023 and 2025.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Country-level deficit scale predicts where currency pressure and protectionist policy responses emerge first — Malaysia's tripling is the steepest adjustment.
insights.quote: The imbalance is regional in scale, but its political consequences are national.
insights.locator: ASEAN's aggregate trade deficit with China rose

themes.theme: U.S. demand as the growth engine

insights.claim: ASEAN exports to the United States grew 37.5% between 2022 and 2025 — roughly five times the pace of exports to China, the EU, Korea, or intra-regional trade — while exports to Japan contracted.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: U.S. final demand, not reshoring, is the dominant driver of ASEAN export growth — U.S. consumer weakness transmits to the region faster than any China slowdown.
insights.locator: Between 2022 and 2025, the region's exports to the United States

insights.claim: ASEAN exports to the United States rose 34% year over year in the first five months of 2026 according to U.S. Census data, despite reshoring rhetoric and escalating tariffs.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Tariffs have not dented ASEAN-to-U.S. volumes — evidence against the thesis that trade policy is successfully repatriating manufacturing.
insights.locator: That momentum continued into 2026

insights.claim: Cambodia sends over 40% of its exports to the United States — mostly garments, footwear, and travel goods — while sourcing 53% of imports from China, largely the fabrics and components those factories consume.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Cambodia is the region's most levered pure pass-through economy and thus the most vulnerable to a U.S. rules-of-origin tightening.
insights.locator: Cambodia sends more than 40% of its exports

insights.claim: Vietnam sends 32% of exports to the U.S. while sourcing 41% of imports from China, and resource-rich Indonesia is the outlier, counting China as both its largest supplier and largest customer.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Indonesia's two-sided China exposure makes it the least tariff-sensitive but most China-cycle-sensitive ASEAN economy — a diversification pair against Vietnam.
insights.locator: Vietnam shows a similar pattern

themes.theme: Chinese inputs embedded in ASEAN manufacturing

insights.claim: China's 2025 export growth to ASEAN was concentrated in manufacturing categories, with electronics imports jumping $57 billion (up 37%), machinery up 30%, metals up 32%, and vehicles up 45%, while only food and fuels declined.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The composition confirms input-feeding rather than consumer dumping in aggregate — but it also means ASEAN factory output is hostage to Chinese export controls.
insights.locator: China's export growth to ASEAN in 2025 was not broad-based

insights.claim: ASEAN runs deficits with China in every major industrial category, with electronics alone at roughly $126 billion and machinery at about $62 billion, while its surpluses are confined to food, agriculture, and fuels.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: ASEAN's trade relationship with China is commodities-out, manufactures-in — an asymmetry that caps the region's industrial value capture.
insights.locator: ASEAN's trade imbalance with China is concentrated in manufactured goods

insights.claim: Federal Reserve researchers characterize the pattern as an asymmetric trade shock in which China's industrial exports expand faster than its demand for manufactured imports.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A named macro frame for the China overcapacity problem: it is a one-way supply impulse, so global manufacturing margins compress wherever it lands.
insights.quote: asymmetric trade shock: China’s industrial exports are expanding faster than its demand for manufactured imports
insights.locator: Federal Reserve researchers describe the broader pattern

insights.claim: Chinese exports of selected manufacturing inputs — printed circuits, electrical switching and connection equipment, cables, transformers, valves, and mechanical transmission components — rose from $10.5 billion in 2017 to $34 billion in 2025, with Vietnam alone taking $13.6 billion.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A more than tripling in eight years quantifies how deeply Chinese components are embedded in the electrical-equipment supply chain feeding U.S. imports.
insights.locator: A closer look at selected manufacturing inputs

insights.claim: Between 2024 and 2025 the U.S. machinery and electronics deficit with China narrowed by about $70 billion while its deficit with ASEAN widened by roughly $80 billion.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Near one-for-one substitution in the U.S. bilateral data — headline China-deficit reduction is largely accounting relocation, not decoupling.
insights.locator: U.S. data point to the same supply-chain reconfiguration

insights.claim: An IMF working paper finds ASEAN exports in tariff-affected categories outperformed other exports through 2022-2023 and expanded beyond the U.S. market, with ASEAN's own global value chain contribution rising alongside greater foreign input use, indicating genuine capacity expansion rather than pure rerouting.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Argues against the pure-transshipment narrative — real industrial capacity is being built in ASEAN, which makes the shift durable through tariff cycles.
insights.locator: An IMF working paper finds that exports

insights.claim: UNCTAD estimates FDI inflows to Southeast Asia rose nearly 10% in 2025 to $244 billion, but much of the increase was concentrated in Singapore.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Headline regional FDI strength overstates the manufacturing story; Singapore's financial and holding-company flows distort the aggregate.
insights.locator: UNCTAD estimates that FDI inflows to Southeast Asia

insights.claim: Announced greenfield investment in Southeast Asia fell for a second straight year to $106 billion, more than 40% below its 2023 peak, and announced investment in GVC-intensive manufacturing more than halved from $31 billion to $14 billion.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The forward pipeline is deteriorating even as current trade flows boom — a leading indicator that ASEAN's export share gains may plateau in 2027-2028.
insights.quote: The contrast suggests that trade reallocation is currently moving faster than the pipeline of new manufacturing investment.
insights.locator: Yet the pipeline of new projects weakened

insights.claim: Investment in Southeast Asia remained concentrated in semiconductors, electronics, AI infrastructure, and data centers even as broader greenfield commitments fell.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Capital is narrowing to AI-adjacent verticals — a bifurcation trade favoring ASEAN semis/data-center names over diversified industrial exposure.
insights.locator: At the same time, investment remained concentrated

themes.theme: Semiconductor flow reversal and the Singapore hub

insights.claim: ASEAN imports of Chinese integrated circuits (HS 8542) reached $49.5 billion in the first half of 2026, up 114%, accounting for more than a third of the total rise in ASEAN imports from China and over half the growth in electronics imports.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: China is now a major chip supplier to ASEAN assembly hubs — a structural change that complicates U.S. export-control enforcement at the packaging layer.
insights.locator: ASEAN's imports of chips from China

insights.claim: ASEAN's direct chip exports to China fell by more than half from $21.6 billion to $10.7 billion, declining in every major market except Singapore, where they more than doubled to $8.9 billion.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The chip trade has flipped direction — Singapore alone is the surviving ASEAN semiconductor conduit into China, concentrating regulatory risk in one node.
insights.locator: ASEAN’s direct chip exports to China moved in the other direction

insights.claim: Chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment together accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in Singapore's exports to China, whose exports to China rose by half in H1 2026 — the fastest growth in the region.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Singapore is functioning as the equipment gateway into China's fabs — a direct exposure for SEMI-cap names routing through the city-state.
insights.locator: Singapore’s exports to China rose by half

insights.claim: Direct ASEAN-China chip trade figures exclude chips reaching China through Hong Kong, which handled more than half of the mainland's semiconductor imports in the first five months of 2026.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Any bilateral chip-trade analysis that ignores the Hong Kong entrepot materially understates flows into China — a caveat for export-control efficacy claims.
insights.locator: These figures cover only direct trade

insights.claim: ASEAN's semiconductor role is expanding mainly in assembly, testing, packaging, and supplier activities — particularly in Malaysia and Vietnam — while leading-edge fabrication stays concentrated in a few advanced economies.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: ASEAN captures the low-margin back end of semis; the value-capture ceiling limits the earnings upside of the region's chip supply-chain equities.
insights.locator: UNCTAD’s investment analysis provides context

insights.claim: Vietnam's exports to China jumped 40% in H1 2026 led by computers and parts supporting China's AI buildout, yet its deficit still reached $56 billion, the region's largest.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Vietnam is now feeding China's AI capex cycle — an underappreciated channel making Vietnamese electronics exports sensitive to Chinese datacenter spending.
insights.locator: Vietnam's exports to China jumped 40%

insights.claim: Malaysia swung from rough balance to a $28 billion shortfall with China in H1 2026 as its chip and fuel sales to China fell, while Thailand's deficit widened fastest, up more than 40% to $36 billion.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Malaysia's chip sales to China are already contracting — a warning sign for Penang-based back-end names dependent on Chinese demand.
insights.locator: The pattern varies across countries

insights.claim: Chinese exports of electric vehicles, batteries, and solar panels to ASEAN totaled nearly $22 billion in 2025, up over 50% from roughly $14 billion and more than six times the 2018 level, with EV exports nearly doubling to $8.2 billion.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: ASEAN has become the fastest-growing outlet for Chinese clean-tech overcapacity — bearish for local EV/solar manufacturers' pricing power.
insights.locator: Chinese exports of electric vehicles, batteries, and solar panels

insights.claim: Chinese clean-tech exports to ASEAN totaled $14.7 billion in H1 2026, 57% above the same period in 2025, with solar-panel shipments more than doubling, batteries up 48%, and EVs up 43%.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Acceleration, not deceleration, in 2026 — Chinese clean-tech export volumes are still compounding and price pressure across the region should intensify.
insights.locator: In the first six months of 2026

insights.claim: The disruption of Gulf oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz in March strengthened the case for renewable-energy deployment across Southeast Asia, though the Chinese clean-tech export surge was already underway before it.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The Hormuz shock adds a persistent energy-security bid under ASEAN solar and storage demand independent of cost curves.
insights.locator: The surge was already underway before the disruption

insights.claim: Chinese clean-tech exports to ASEAN are highly concentrated by product and geography: Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand take over 60% of the 2025 total, Vietnam's $5.6 billion is 88% batteries, Indonesia leads in both EVs and solar, and the Philippines and Laos are solar-skewed.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Each ASEAN market faces a different clean-tech competition problem, so policy responses (tariffs, local-content rules) will be country- and product-specific.
insights.locator: China’s clean-tech exports to ASEAN were concentrated

insights.claim: Cheap Chinese EVs, batteries, and solar panels lower the cost of ASEAN's energy and transport transitions while simultaneously undercutting local producers and blocking governments' attempts to build domestic clean-tech industries.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The consumption-versus-industrial-policy tradeoff determines whether ASEAN erects clean-tech barriers — watch local-content mandates in Indonesia and Thailand.
insights.locator: Clean technology exports present ASEAN governments

insights.claim: ASEAN governments must simultaneously avoid high U.S. tariffs, manage China's export surge, and preserve access to Chinese inputs that keep their exports competitive — three objectives that are increasingly irreconcilable.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The trilemma implies rising policy volatility in ASEAN capitals; one objective must eventually be sacrificed, most likely input openness.
insights.locator: The balancing act is getting harder

insights.claim: Southeast Asia is becoming a critical production layer between Chinese industrial supply and global demand rather than a substitute for China, producing a deeper and more geographically dispersed form of integration.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Supply-chain risk has been dispersed geographically but not reduced — a China input disruption still propagates to U.S. shelves via ASEAN.
insights.locator: The chip trade distills a broader story

insights.claim: ASEAN economies are not choosing between China and the United States but managing an economic model structurally dependent on both simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Expect hedging and non-alignment to persist regardless of U.S. pressure — bets on ASEAN picking a side are likely to be wrong.
insights.quote: ASEAN governments are therefore not choosing between China and the United States so much as managing an economic model that depends on both.
insights.locator: That position brings gains and exposure
